To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we observed DNA translocation by EcoR124I and that we found that EcoR124I is able to track along the helical path of DNA.
EcoR124I, an example of a type I restriction enzyme and a member of superfamily 2 of helicases, is able to translocate DNA at a rate of ~ 1 bp/s.
the EcoR124I motor translocates at a rate of ~ 1 base pair (bp) per second, and it tracks along the helix.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of DNA translocation in type I enzymes.
the mechanism of DNA translocation, and the role of the motor domains in DNA translocation.
the mechanochemical properties of DNA translocases and their implications for the mechanism of translocation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EcoR124I is a highly processive DNA translocase with a translocation step of 10 bp.
EcoR124I, like other SF2 helicases, translocates DNA along a single strand of DNA in a processive, ATP-dependent manner.
EcoR124I is a processive motor that translocates along the DNA double helix in a direction opposite to that of the DNA helix.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the type I restriction enzymes EcoR124I and EcoR124II are the first members of SF2 that are characterized at the single-molecule level.
EcoR124I translocates DNA by using a Brownian ratchet mechanism, in which the enzyme steps along DNA by binding and unbinding to DNA in a sequence-dependent manner.
EcoR124I, as a member of SF2, is a force-generating motor that can track DNA in the 5'-3' direction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EcoR124I is a highly processive DNA translocase.

EcoR124I is a robust, well-behaved motor protein that can be used to study DNA translocation in real time.
